# Cooperation of the ATM and Fanconi Anemia/BRCA Pathways in Double-Strand Break End Resection

**Authors:** Mu-Yan Cai; Connor E. Dunn; Wenxu Chen; Bose S. Kochupurakkal; Huy Nguyen; Lisa A. Moreau; Geoffrey I. Shapiro; Kalindi Parmar; David Kozono; Alan D. D’Andrea

**Affiliations:** 1Department of Radiation Oncology, Dana-Farber Cancer Institute, Boston, MA 02215, USA | 2Collaborative Innovation Center for Cancer Medicine, State Key Laboratory of Oncology in South China, Sun Yat-sen University Cancer Center, Guangzhou 510060, China | 3Center for DNA Damage and Repair, Dana-Farber Cancer Institute, Boston, MA 02215, USA | 4Early Drug Development Center, Dana-Farber Cancer Institute, Boston, MA 02215, USA | 5Lead Contact

## Abstract

Cells deficient in ataxia telangiectasia mutated (ATM) are hypersensitive to ionizing radiation and other anti-cancer agents that induce double-strand DNA breaks. ATM inhibitors may therefore sensitize cancer cells to these agents. Some cancers may also have underlying genetic defects predisposing them to an ATM inhibitor monotherapy response. We have conducted a genome-wide CRISPR screen to identify genetic vulnerabilities that sensitize lung cancer cells to ATM inhibitors. Knockout of genes in the Fanconi anemia (FA)/BRCA pathway results in hypersensitivity to the ATM inhibitor M3541. Knockdown of either an FA gene or of ATM results in reduced double-strand break end resection, enhanced non-homologous end joining (NHEJ) repair, and decreased homologous recombination repair. Knockout of both the FA/BRCA pathway and ATM strongly inhibits end resection and generates toxic levels of NHEJ, thereby elucidating a mechanism of cellular death by synthetic lethality. ATM inhibitors may therefore be useful for the treatment of tumors with a defective FA/BRCA pathway.

## Abstract

ATM inhibitors are currently in clinical development as anti-cancer agents. Using a genome-wide CRISPR screen, Cai et al. demonstrate that cancer cells with Fanconi anemia (FA) pathway deficiency are sensitive to ATM inhibition. The authors also show that synthetic lethality between ATM and the FA pathway is due to reduced DNA resection and increased toxic NHEJ.

## Abstract

## INTRODUCTION

The ataxia telangiectasia mutated (ATM) kinase is a master regulator of the DNA damage response (DDR) (Shiloh and Ziv, 2013), and multiple ATM substrates have been identified. Mutations in the ATM gene result in hypersensitivity to ionizing radiation (IR) and to other DNA damaging agents. ATM coordinates the activity of two DNA double-strand break (DSB) repair pathways, namely, the homologous recombination (HR) pathway and the non-homologous end joining (NHEJ) pathway. Mutations in the ATM gene result in discordant activity of these pathways, persistent DSBs, and genomic instability. Consistent with these cellular phenotypes, humans or mice with biallelic ATM mutations are predisposed to cancers (Swift and Su, 1999).

Since ATM plays such a central role in the DDR, pharmacologic inhibition of ATM is an attractive opportunity for cancer therapy (Batey et al., 2013; Hickson et al., 2004). Nonspecific drugs, such as wortmannin, inhibit ATM and cause radiosensitization; however, this agent also targets other members of the PIKK (phosphatidylinositol-3-kinase-like kinase) family, including DNA-PK (DNA-dependent protein kinase) and ATR (ataxia telangiectasia and Rad3-related protein). KU-559333, another ATM inhibitor (ATMi) (Batey et al., 2013), does not target other PIKKs at effective concentrations; however, early clinical trials have not progressed due to off-target side effects. A recent compound, M3541, is a highly specific and potent inhibitor of ATM (Zimmermann et al., 2018), and a National Cancer Institute (NCI) clinical trial was recently initiated with the drug in combination with radiotherapy (NCT03225105).

Human cancers with an underlying defect in one DNA repair pathway may be hyperdependent on a second pathway. For example, BRCA1/2-deficient tumors with a defect in the HR pathway are hyperdependent on a polyADP ribose polymerase (PARP1)-dependent repair pathway. Accordingly, PARP1 inhibition has proven clinical efficacy in BRCA1/2 mutant ovarian and breast cancer (Bryant et al., 2005; Farmer et al., 2005), and four PARP1 inhibitors have now been granted limited FDA approval. Whether tumors with a deficiency of the ATM pathway also have specific synthetic lethal relationships with other DNA repair pathways remains largely unknown.

In the current study, we performed a genome-wide clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats (CRISPR)-Cas9 loss-of-function genetic screen to identify enhancers of cell killing by the ATMi M3541 (Zimmermann et al., 2018). Notably, single guide RNAs (sgRNAs) directed against multiple genes in the Fanconi anemia (FA)/BRCA pathway (Ceccaldi et al., 2016b; Rodríguez and D’Andrea, 2017)—including FANCA, FANCF, and FANCG—and FA-like genes—including FAAP24, FAAP100, and FANCM—were synthetic lethal with ATM. sgRNAs directed against additional DNA repair genes including PTEN, Rad18, and STAG2 also conferred ATMi hypersensitivity. These genes are not FA genes per se, but their knockdown has previously been shown to confer DNA crosslinker sensitivity. Concurrent knockdown of both the FA/BRCA pathway and the ATM pathway resulted in reduced DSB end resection, hyperactivation of NHEJ repair, and enhanced chromosome aberrations, thereby elucidating a mechanism of the synthetic lethality. Inhibition of NHEJ activity in tumor cells with a dual disruption of the FA/BRCA and ATM pathways restored cell survival. Taken together, our results suggest that the FA/BRCA pathway and the ATM pathway play redundant functions in enhancing DSB resection and suppressing NHEJ. We hypothesize that human tumors with an underlying defect in the FA/BRCA pathway may be hypersensitive to ATMis. Moreover, understanding the potential sensitivity and resistance mechanisms of ATMis may be useful in predicting patient responses, designing ATMi therapy combinations, and implementing mechanisms of re-sensitization.

## RESULTS

### Identification of sgRNAs That Selectively Enhance or Suppress Cell Killing by ATMi M3541

Initially, we evaluated A549 and NCI-H460 (H460) non-small cell lung cancer cell (NSCLC) lines, which stably express the Cas9 endonuclease. Using a clonogenic assay, we analyzed the cytotoxicity resulting from a combination of M3541—or of another ATMi, KU59333—with IR in these cells (Figures S1A and S1B). In accordance with previous studies, minimal toxicity was observed from ATMi exposure alone, with concentrations ranging up to 1.0 μM of drug. Enhanced cytotoxicity, however, was observed upon subsequent exposure to 2–6 Gy doses of IR. IR is known to rapidly activate the phosphorylation of ATM at Ser1981 (Bakkenist and Kastan, 2003). Low doses of M3541 or KU59333, in the micromolar range, resulted in a decrease in pS1981 over 2 h post-drug exposure in both the A549 and H460 cell lines (Figure S1C).

We next devised a genome-wide CRISPR screen to identify genes that, when disrupted, enhance or suppress cell killing by the ATMi M3541 (Figure 1). We reasoned that sgRNAs directed against specific genes would either enhance or suppress cell killing by M3541. The screen was conducted in the A549 and H460 cell lines, in the presence or absence of the ATMi M3541. The A549 and H460 cell lines are wild type (WT) for both ATM and the pro-apoptotic gene, p53.

In order to identify sgRNAs that target genes involved in both sensitivity and resistance to M3541, we chose a moderate concentration of the drug that inhibits the phosphorylation of ATM at Ser1981 at a low concentration (1 μM). Cells were infected with the Brunello v2 lentiviral sgRNA library and grown for 19 days in media treated with DMSO or the ATMi M3541 (Figure 1A). Fresh media, with freshly dissolved drug, were added every 3 days. Cells were collected pre- and post-drug selection, genomic DNA was extracted, and sgRNA sequences were PCR amplified and Illumina sequenced. Top hits among gene knockouts that conferred drug sensitivity or resistance were identified.

To identify highly significant hits, we utilized a STAR score at ≥4 when analyzing a single cell line. We included hits with a STAR score at ≥2 when analyzing the two cell lines together. The screen identified 62 genes in the A549 cell line and 38 genes in the H460 cell line that modulated cell killing by M3541. Out of these hits, we identified 30 genes that were hits in both cell lines. Many hits corresponded to specific signaling pathways (Figure 1B), and the top hits were DNA repair pathways. Gene Ontology analysis of 70 gene sets revealed strong enrichment for biological processes linked to the FA/BRCA pathway, a DNA crosslink repair pathway composed of 23 known FA genes (Ceccaldi et al., 2016b; Rodríguez and D’Andrea, 2017). Mapping the 70-gene set on the HumanMine protein-protein interaction database created a highly connected network consisting of multiple DNA damage repair genes, including most of the members of the FA/BRCA pathway (Figure 1C).

Many of the same genes that modulate M3541-mediated cell killing were identified in both lung cancer cell lines (see Figures 1D [scatterplot] and S1D [volcano plots] for the A549 and H460 cell lines). Top hits included FAAP24, FAAP100, FANCF, FANCE, FANCI, FANCA, FANCG, FANCB, FANCC, and FANCD2. Other relevant top hits included RAD18, an E3 ligase known to monoubiquitinate and activate FANCD2 (Williams et al., 2011); the tumor suppressor gene PTEN (McCabe et al., 2015); and the cohesin protein STAG2 (Watrin and Peters, 2009). These genes have also previously been shown to regulate DNA repair processes.

Several genes that regulate DNA DSB end resection were also hits in the screen. Knockdown of CtIP, a known phosphorylation target of ATM (Duquette et al., 2012), and knockdown of EXO1 were synthetic lethal with the ATMi (Figure 1D, lower left quadrant). While CtIP is not an FA gene, per se, it is known to bind to FANCD2 (Murina et al., 2014; Unno et al., 2014; Yeo et al., 2014). Knockdown of either FA/BRCA genes or of nucleases involved in DSB end resection, such as MRE11, conferred cellular hypersensitivity to the ATMi. Accordingly, our results implied that the FA/BRCA pathway and the ATM pathway may directly or indirectly regulate the DSB end resection through interactions with resection nucleases. Moreover, knockdowns of components of the ATM activating MRN complex (Wang et al., 2013), including Rad50 and NBS1, were also hits in the screen.

Interestingly, sgRNAs directed against components of the BRCA1-A complex (including BABAM1, BABAM2, and ABRAXAS1) were shown to increase the growth of both A549 and H460 cells grown in the presence of the ATMi (Figures 1D [upper right quadrant] and S1D). This functional interaction of ATM with subunits of the BRCA1-A complex has been recently demonstrated (Balmus et al., 2019). The BRCA1-A complex is known to suppress HR repair (Balmus et al., 2019; Harris and Khanna, 2011; Sobhian et al., 2007). The loss of this pathway may enhance the HR and increase resistance to ATM inhibition. This finding further supports an underlying role of ATM in enhancing HR repair. Finally, sgRNA directed against ATM itself protected cells treated with M3541. This result further validates the screen and provides further evidence that the ATMi is specific and is acting through its specific target. Loss of a drug target is a common mechanism of acquired drug resistance (Pettitt et al., 2018).

### Concomitant Loss of the FA/BRCA Pathway and ATM Function Is Toxic to Cells

We previously demonstrated that a small interfering RNA (siRNA) directed against the FA protein FANCG is synthetically lethal with ATM loss (Kennedy et al., 2007). Whether ATM knockdown is also synthetically lethal with the loss of other genes in the FA/BRCA pathway is unknown. We next validated the CRISPR screen results by CRISPR knockout of individual FA genes and of FA-associated genes FAAP24 (Figures S2A and 2A), FAAP100 (Figures S2A and 2B), and FANCF (Figures S2A and 2C) in A549 and H460 cells. Protein knockdown by CRISPR knockout was confirmed by immunoblotting with the corresponding antibodies. As expected, knockout of these individual genes resulted in enhanced sensitivity to the ATMi. We next validated synthetic lethality relationships between the ATM and these genes along with RAD18 and PTEN (Figures S2B and S2C). The siRNA-mediated knockdown of FAAP24, FAAP100, FANCF, RAD18, or PTEN in A549 and NCI-H460 cells resulted in cellular sensitivity to the ATMi, as predicted by the CRISPR screen results. We next determined whether the synthetic lethal relationship of FA genes and ATM could be extended to other cell types. Indeed, knockout of the FA genes FANCA and FANCD2 in HeLa and U2OS cells, respectively, conferred sensitivity to the ATMi, further validating the CRISPR screen results and extending the data (Figures S2A and 2D).

### Mechanism of Synthetic Lethality between the FA Pathway and ATM Pathway

To determine the mechanism of synthetic lethality in cells with a dual knockdown of the FA pathway and ATM, we examined various DNA repair biomarkers (Figure 3). Initially, we examined HeLa cells or U2OS cells that have a CRISPR-engineered knockout of either FANCA or FANCD2, respectively. Knockout of FANCA or FANCD2 in either cell line resulted in increased DNA DSB, as measured by IR-induced H2AX phosphorylation (Figure 3A). Breakage was enhanced by exposure to ATMi, perhaps resulting from slower DNA repair kinetics. In a comet assay, we also observed longer tails, reflecting increased DNA damage following treatment with the ATMi in the FA-deficient HeLa and U2OS cell lines (Figures S3A and S3B).

We next determined whether the loss of a gene in the FA pathway could confer a reduction in HR repair in these cell lines. Previous studies have indicated that FA gene knockdown can result in a mild reduction in both HR activity and single-strand annealing (SSA) (Nakanishi et al., 2005). Indeed, FANCA or FANCD2 knockout in either HeLa cells or U2OS cells resulted in decreased IR-induced RAD51 foci (Figure 3B). The level of RAD51 focus formation is a measure of BRCA2/RAD51 loading and HR competence. Interestingly, exposure of FANCA-deficient or FANCD2-deficient cells to the ATMi M3541 resulted in a further loss of RAD51 foci (Figure 3B). Taken together, these results indicate that the FA pathway and the ATM pathway each contribute positively to HR repair. We hypothesized that the loss of both pathways would cause a profound loss of HR repair, further contributing to the lethal phenotypes observed when both pathways are compromised.

Knockdown of FANCA or FANCD2 resulted in decreased DNA DSB resection and decreased single-stranded DNA (ssDNA) generation, as demonstrated by decreased IR-induced replication factor A (RPA) foci (Figure 3C). The decrease in RPA foci following FA gene knockdown suggests that the FA pathway—through its interaction with various resection proteins, such as CtIP and EXO1—can positively regulate the process of end resection and HR repair. In contrast, changes in IR-induced 53BP1 foci were not observed when comparing vehicle control and ATMi treated FANCA−/− or FANCD2−/− cells (Figure 3D).

FANCA-deficient cells exhibited enhanced ATM phosphorylation (Figure S3C), consistent with the synthetic lethality observed when both pathways are disrupted. This increased pATM level suggests that in the absence of the FA/BRCA pathway, cells are hyperdependent on activation of the ATM pathway for survival. Similarly, the loss of ATM resulted in hyperactivation of the FA/BRCA pathway, as detected by elevated FANCD2 monoubiquitination (Figure S3D). Again, these results further support a synthetic lethal relationship of these two pathways. When one pathway is knocked down, the other pathway is upregulated.

### Knockout of the FA and ATM Pathways Reduces DSB End Resection, Increases End Joining, and Increases NHEJ

Recent studies demonstrate that the cellular choice between HR repair and NHEJ repair of DSBs is determined by the process of DSB end resection (Ceccaldi et al., 2016a; Symington, 2016). Increased resection favors HR, while the blockage of resection favors NHEJ. We next evaluated the role of the FA and ATM pathways in end resection by using several independent assays.

End resection of a DSB by nucleolytic degradation of the 5′ strand is the first step in initiating the HR pathway. The exposed 3′ single-strand DNA binds to RPA, which in turn is displaced by the recombinase, RAD51. Previous studies have shown that the ATM kinase can promote DSB end resection by phosphorylating and activating the protein CtIP (Duquette et al., 2012). Other studies have independently shown that monoubiquitinated FANCD2, the downstream regulator in the FA pathway, can recruit CtIP to chromatin and further promote DSB end resection (Murina et al., 2014; Unno et al., 2014; Yeo et al., 2014).

To directly determine the role of FA and ATM in DSB resection, we labeled genomic DNA with 5-bromo-2′-deoxyuridine (BrdU) and used an antibody that detects ssDNA resulting from end resection. Knockout of FANCD2 decreased BrdU-positive cells, and inhibition of ATM with M3541 further impaired IR-induced BrdU focus formation in FANCD2−/− cells (Figure 4A).

To further quantify the extent of resection, we introduced the AsiSI enzyme fused with a hormone-binding domain in U2OS cells with either FANCD2 or FANCF knockdown. A quantitative PCR (qPCR)-based method was used to examine ssDNA (Figure 4B). A decrease in the amount of ssDNA was found after the depletion of FANCF or of FANCD2. A further decrease in the level of ssDNA was observed following the depletion of both the FA/BRCA pathway and the ATM pathway.

Next, we performed a SMART (single-molecule analysis of resection tracks) assay to further evaluate the effect of FA pathway disruption and/or ATM inhibition on DSB end resection (Figures 4C and S4A). This assay quantifies the amount of ssDNA generated by end resection at a defined DSB (Huertas and Cruz-García, 2018). Disruption of the FANCD2 gene resulted in a minor reduction in DSB end resection, as did exposure to the ATMi. Interestingly, dual disruption of the FA/BRCA and ATM pathways resulted in a further decrease in DSB end resection, consistent with the enhancement of toxic NHEJ activity observed when both pathways are knocked down. Moreover, complementation with FANCD2 in FANCD2-KO cells rescued this phenotype (Figure S4B). Consistent with previous studies, these results indicate that the FA/BRCA pathway normally promotes DSB end resection, leading to a suppression of NHEJ. We next determined whether the FA pathway is required for the recruitment of CtIP to chromatin and whether ATM further promotes this recruitment (Figures 4D and S4C). Interestingly, knockout of FANCD2 (Figure 4D) or of FANCA (Figure S4C) reduced CtIP expression (lanes 3 and 4) and chromatin recruitment of CtIP (lanes 11 and 12), and ATMi further reduced CtIP recruitment. CtIP knockdown resulted in reduced survival of WT U2OS cells. CtIP knockdown resulted in increased toxicity, however, in FANCD2 knockout U2OS cells, suggesting a synthetic lethality between CtIP and FANCD2. Overexpression of CtIP rescued the lethality in both the WT and FANCD2 knockout U2OS cells (Figure S4D). Taken together, these results further demonstrate that the FA and ATM pathways cooperate in enhancing CtIP mediated end resection.

### Knockdown of the FA Pathway Results in Increased NHEJ Activity and Decreased HR Activity

Previous studies have suggested that NHEJ is upregulated in cells deficient in the FA pathway (Adamo et al., 2010; Eccles et al., 2018; Pace et al., 2010). Knockdown of components of the NHEJ pathway, such as DNA-PK (Adamo et al., 2010) or DNA ligase 4 (Maruyama et al., 2015), reduces the interstrand crosslinker (ICL) sensitivity of FA cells. Recent studies also indicate that NHEJ is upregulated in ATM-deficient cells (Balmus et al., 2019), suggesting that a principal cellular function of ATM is to suppress the NHEJ pathway and to promote DSB end resection and HR. Knockdown of the HR-suppressing BRCA1-A complex can enhance resistance to ATMi (Balmus et al., 2019).

Based on these studies and our evidence of synthetic lethality between FA and ATM, we reasoned that the mechanism of synthetic lethality is a decrease in DSB end resection, an increase in end joining, and an increase in toxic NHEJ following FA and ATM knockdown. Previous studies have indicated that either the FA pathway or ATM is required to remove NHEJ proteins, such as 53BP1, from DSBs that have been generated in the process of DNA crosslink repair or by nuclease processing of reversed forks. We reasoned that loss of both the FA pathway and ATM would further inhibit DSB resection, increase end joining, and further upregulate NHEJ.

To further examine whether the ATMi promotes NHEJ, we used an NHEJ reporter template (Figure 5; Howard et al., 2015). Knockdown of components of the FA/BRCA pathway, including BRCA1, FAAP24, or FANCD2, in U2OS cells increased NHEJ activity. Efficient knockdown of the FA proteins was confirmed by immunoblot. Knockdown of FA protein expression resulted in an enhancement of NHEJ activity. Cellular exposure to the ATMi further increased NHEJ activity in these cells (Figure 5A).

Interestingly, knockdown of the FA pathway and ATM resulted in a decrease in HR, as measured by the DR-GFP assay (Figure 5B). As further evidence to support this mechanism, knockout of FANCA in HeLa cells (Figure S5A), or knockout of FANCD2 in U2OS cells (Figure S5B), resulted in increased phosphorylation of DNA-PK (pDNA-PK), a biomarker of the activated NHEJ pathway. The addition of ATMi further increased pDNA-PK and DNA damage, as measured by pH2AX (Figures S5A and S5B). Taken together, these results indicate that the FA pathway and the ATM pathway are non-epistatic, and each suppresses NHEJ activity. Knocking down both pathways resulted in excessive end-joining activity and cellular death, providing additional mechanistic evidence for synthetic lethality.

### ATM Is Required for Homologous Recombination Repair in FA/BRCA-Pathway-Deficient Cells

FA-pathway-deficient cells and ATM-deficient cells have a common cellular phenotype, namely, the accumulation of chromosome radial forms. Indeed, the diagnostic test for FA is the DEB (diepoxybutane) or mitomycin C (MMC)-induced increase in chromosome radials. Chromosome radials result from hyperactive non-homologous pairing of chromosomes, indirectly resulting from increased NHEJ activity (Newell et al., 2004). BRCA1-deficient cells exposed to PARP inhibitors exhibit elevated radial chromosomes (Bunting and Nussenzweig, 2010). Knockout of multiple components of the NHEJ pathway, such as the 53BP1 or SHLD complex subunits, in BRCA1-deficient cells results in a reduction of radial chromosomes and in enhanced cell survival (Mirman et al., 2018).

We next determined whether a disruption of ATM activity would further increase NHEJ activity, chromosome aberrations, and radial formation in FA cells (Figure 6). For this purpose, we examined the effect of ATMi exposure on the FANCG-deficient lymphoblast line, PD326. M3541 increased chromosome radials in PD326 cells, consistent with an enhancement of toxic NHEJ activity. ATMi plus the crosslinker, MMC, further enhanced chromosome radial production. Interestingly, an inhibitor of DNA ligase IV, a downstream enzyme in the NHEJ pathway, reduced chromosome radials, further indicating that the increased radial production resulted from decreased end resection and increased end joining activity (Figures 6A and 6B). As a control, ATMi or MMC exposure did not induce chromosome aberrations or radials in the corrected isogenic cell line, PD326 plus FANCG (Figure 6C). The inhibitor of DNA ligase IV also enhanced clonogenic survival of other FA-pathway-deficient cells, including the FANCA-deficient and FANCD2-deficient cells, when they were exposed to ATMi (Figures S6A and S6B).

### Synthetic Lethality of FA Pathway and ATM in Human Cancer Cell Lines

FA pathway disruption is observed in many human cancers, including pancreatic cancer (van der Heijden et al., 2005) and ovarian cancer (Taniguchi et al., 2003). The FA-pathway-deficient pancreatic cancer cell lines PL11 and HS766T were sensitive to the ATMi. Decreased expression of the FANCC protein in PL11 cells and decreased expression of the FANCG protein in the HS766T cell line were confirmed by immunoblotting with the corresponding antibodies. The cDNA-complemented versions of these cell lines exhibited decreased sensitivity to the ATMi (Figures 7A and 7B). The TOV21G cell line is an ovarian cancer line exhibiting methylation and silencing of the FANCF gene (Taniguchi et al., 2003). An isogenic line TOV21G+FANCF has an intact FA pathway. As predicted, the TOV21G cells were more sensitive to ATMi exposure (Figure 7C) than were the complemented cells. Finally, BRCA1-deficient cells that had acquired resistance to the PARP inhibitor, olaparib, were sensitized by the addition of the ATMi (Figures 7D and 7E).

### Validation of Synthetic Lethality of FA and ATM Pathways Using Computational Approaches

Analysis of publicly available tumor and cell line databases was conducted to further validate the synthetic lethal relationship between the FA and ATM pathways. We initially focused on genes that, when lost or mutated, sensitized cells to the ATMi (M3541) in our CRISPR screen. The gene hits with an average -log10(P) < 2.5 and an average log2 fold change of at least 0.5, in both A549 and H460 cells, were RAD18, FAAP24, FAAP100, and FANCF (Figure S1D). Analysis of a cancer-dependency study revealed that cell lines with copy number loss of any one of these four genes, but not cell lines with normal copy number of these genes, are hyperdependent on ATM for survival. (Figure S7A). Moreover, cell lines with mutations in genes encoding proteins in the FA core complex proteins are more dependent on ATM for survival than are the cell lines that are the WT for these genes (Figure S7B).

MMC is a chemotherapeutic agent known to cause DNA crosslinks. Crosslinks are repaired, in part, by the FA pathway. Cells lacking a functional FA pathway are deficient in crosslink repair and are hypersensitive to MMC. As described above, cells lacking the FA pathway are also sensitive to ATMi. We therefore investigated a possible correlation between cellular sensitivity to MMC and ATMi using a drug sensitivity database. Indeed, the cell lines that are sensitive to MMC tend to be more sensitive to the ATMi KU-55933, corroborating the notion that a loss of the FA pathway results in sensitivity to both an ATMi and MMC (Figure S7C).

The synthetic lethal relationship between the FA pathway and ATM described here suggests that cells with defects in both the FA pathway and ATM may not be viable. Tumors with co-occurrence of FA and ATM mutations are therefore hypothesized to have reduced viability. In order to test this hypothesis, we analyzed clinical data from the PanCancer MSK-IMPACT Clinical Sequencing Cohort. Interestingly, the patients with tumors harboring mutations in both the FA pathway and ATM showed significantly improved survival by a log-rank test, compared to the patients with tumors that are WT for these genes (Figure S7D). Taken together, computational analysis of publicly available databases supports the synthetic lethality between the FA pathway and ATMi observed in the CRISPR screen.

## DISCUSSION

Cancer cells have multiple DNA repair pathways for coping with intrinsic DNA damage and replication stress. These cells often lose one or more of these pathways through mutation, deletion, or epigenetic silencing, resulting in genomic instability, a mutator phenotype, and a more rapidly evolving malignancy. Cells with one dysfunctional DNA repair pathway may become hyperdependent on an alternative pathway for survival. For instance, tumor cells with a loss of BRCA1 and BRCA2, required for HR repair, are hyperdependent on PARP1-dependent DNA repair mechanisms such as base excision repair (BER) (Lord and Ashworth, 2016) or alternative end joining (Alt-EJ) (Ceccaldi et al., 2015; Mateos-Gomez et al., 2015). Accordingly, inhibitors of PARP or other components of the Alt-EJ pathway, such as POLQ (Higgins and Boulton, 2018), may be cytotoxic to HR-deficient tumor cells.

In the current study, we sought to identify genetic vulnerabilities in cancer cell lines that are predisposed to cell death by ATMi monotherapy. We demonstrated that a disruption of the FA/BRCA pathway enhances cell killing by M3541. Further disruption of the terminal components of cNHEJ can reduce the cell killing. Moreover, we demonstrate that one mechanism of the synthetic lethality resulting from a dual disruption of ATM and FA pathway genesis elevated (toxic) cNHEJ activity and decreased HR activity.

Previous studies have suggested that elevated NHEJ activity may account for the cellular features of FA cells. FA cells have elevated ICL sensitivity and an elevation in ICL-induced chromosome radial forms. These radial forms result from enhanced non-homologous pairing of chromosomes, as evident in metaphase chromosome spreads (Newell et al., 2004). Previous studies have also indicated that FA proteins or ATM can function, at least in part, by excluding or removing NHEJ proteins, such as 53BP1, from the sites of DSBs. These breaks may occur during ICL repair or during nuclease processing of reversed replication forks. Loss of both the FA pathway and ATM results in further retention of NHEJ factors at DSBs and persistence of NHEJ activity, extending even into the S phase of the cell cycle. This toxic NHEJ can cause the inappropriate fusion of DNA breaks on different chromosomes. Indeed, the radial chromosomes resulting from fused segments of non-homologous chromosomes resemble the genomic rearrangements found in primary cells from FA patients. Interestingly, this increase in non-homologous pairing correlates with increased NHEJ activity (Adamo et al., 2010; Eccles et al., 2018; Pace et al., 2010). Consistent with this model, a knockdown of NHEJ activity, resulting from cellular exposure to a DNA-PK inhibitor or inhibition of ligase 4, can reverse this phenotype and reduce the ICL sensitivity of FA cells.

ATM is known to promote DSB end resection and suppress NHEJ. The enhancement of DSB end resection results, at least in part, from the ability of ATM to inactivate the 53BP1/RIF1/REV7/SHLD complex, thereby enabling DSB end resection, RAD51 loading, and homologous recombination. Our results indicate that the FA pathway also promotes DSB end resection, although the mechanism of enhanced resection remains unknown. Monoubiquitinated FANCD2, a downstream product of the FA pathway, may bind and stimulate the end resection activity of CtIP. Recent studies also indicate that the FANCA protein can promote the process of SSA (Benitez et al., 2018) and may thereby positively regulate end resection. Accordingly, inactivation of both the ATM and FA pathways appears to further reduce DSB end resection. Inactivation of both pathways simultaneously results in a further decrease in end resection, accounting for the enhancement of NHEJ activity and further contributing to synthetic lethality.

Our results indicate that ATM and the FA pathway cooperate in the regulation of DSB end resection. We previously demonstrated a convergence of this pathway in DNA crosslink repair (Taniguchi et al., 2002). The current study supports a model for the regulation of DSB end resection (Figure S7E). The FA pathway promotes the monoubiquitination and chromatin recruitment of FANCD2. FANCD2-Ub binds to and promotes the chromatin recruitment of CtIP to the site of DSB end resection. ATM further phosphorylates and activates CtIP. Activated CtIP next promotes DSB end resection and suppresses NHEJ. This model provides one of the mechanisms for the synthetic lethal relationship of FA genes and ATM. Loss of both pathways leads to a profound reduction in DSB end resection, leading to toxic NHEJ, as indicated by radial chromosome accumulation.

Our results also suggest that tumor cells may become resistant to an ATMi by finding an alternate mechanism for enhancing DSB end resection, such as by knocking down the BRCA1-A complex or by reducing NHEJ levels. FA cells corresponding to some FA complementation groups also have reduced HR activity and increased PARPi sensitivity. In our study, simultaneous disruption of the FA pathway and ATM resulted in a profound decrease in RAD51 focus formation and cell death, thereby providing a second mechanism of synthetic lethality. Interestingly, the loss of the BRCA1-A complex, a complex known to suppress HR repair, can rescue RAD51 foci, restore HR repair, and rescue cell viability, based on our CRISPR screen results. Accordingly, our CRISPR screen identified components of the BRCA1-A complex, which, when knocked out, enhanced the viability of A549 or H460 cells exposed to the ATMi.

In addition to bona fide members of the FA/BRCA pathway, we identified other genes whose loss is synthetically lethal with ATMi. RAD18 is a ubiquitin E3 ligase known to monoubiquitinate PCNA and to activate TLS (translesion synthesis) repair. Interestingly, RAD18 may also play a role in FA/BRCA pathway function. In one study, RAD18 was shown to promote the FA core complex-dependent monoubiquitination of FANCD2 in a manner that is secondary to its ability to monoubiquitinate PCNA (Song et al., 2010). Moreover, RAD18 was shown to bind to FANCD2 and to promote the monoubiquitination of the FANCD2/FANCI complex (Williams et al., 2011).

The tumor suppressor protein PTEN has also been reported to have a role in the DDR (Gupta et al., 2009; Shen et al., 2007). Loss of PTEN function underlies some cancers, such as prostate cancer and glioblastoma (Li et al., 1997). In addition to its cytoplasmic role in the PI3K pathway, PTEN functions as a nuclear protein and appears to have a direct function in DNA repair. Cells with a deficiency in nuclear targeting of PTEN are defective in HR repair and, like FA cells, are sensitive to DNA crosslinking agents such as cisplatin (Bassi et al., 2013). A recent report further supports a model in which PTEN loss is synthetically lethal with loss of the ATM kinase (McCabe et al., 2015).

STAG2 is a core component of the cohesin complex, which also includes SMC1, SMC2, and Rad21 (Watrin and Peters, 2009). The cohesin complex is required for optimal DNA repair, including DSB repair, in human cells (Terret et al., 2009; Tittel-Elmer et al., 2012). The cohesin complex is known to organize chromatin loops at DNA replication factories, to mediate replication stress tolerance, and to enhance the restart of stalled forks (Wu and Yu, 2012). Somatic mutation of STAG2 in some cancers accounts for crosslinker-dependent chromosome breakage and cisplatin sensitivity, a phenotype similar to cancers with FA/BRCA pathway deficiency (Stoepker et al., 2015). Interestingly, STAG2 also plays a role in replication fork progression and has a synthetic lethal relationship with PARP and ATR loss in DSB repair (Mondal et al., 2019). Taken together, these results are consistent with the synthetic lethal relationship of STAG2 and ATM described herein.

In summary, tumor cells that have an underlying genetic or epigenetic defect in the FA pathway—or in RAD18, PTEN, or STAG2—may be hypersensitive to the ATMi M3541. Accordingly, patients bearing tumors with these defects may be more likely to respond to the ATMi, and these patients may be more likely to benefit from it.

### METHODS DETAILS

#### Drug selection CRISPR screens

NSCLC cell lines A549 and NCI-H460 stably expressing the Cas9 endonuclease (pXPR_311) were obtained from the Genetic Perturbation Platform at the Broad Institute. The lines were grown at 37°C in a humidified 5% CO2 incubator in GIBCO RPMI 1640 (Life Technologies, Grand Island, NY) supplemented with 10% fetal bovine serum (FBS, Sigma-Aldrich, St. Louis, MO) and 100 μg/ml Normocin (InvivoGen, San Diego, CA). The pXPR_311 plasmid contains a blasticidin resistance tag to allow for selection of infected cells. For each line, the selected Cas9 positive cells were infected in four 12-well tissue culture plates with the Brunello whole genome sgRNA pooled lentiviral library consisting of 76,441 sgRNAs targeting 19,114 different genes (Doench et al., 2016). For adequate representation of each sgRNA, e.g., an average of 500 cells/sgRNA, a total of 135 million cells divided into wells each containing 3 million cells were infected at a multiplicity of infection (MOI) of 0.3 in media containing 8 μg/ml polybrene. Plates were centrifuged at 2000 rpm for 2 hours at 37°C, and then 2 hours after centrifugation, media was replaced with fresh media without polybrene and cells were incubated overnight. Infected cells were transferred to 15 cm tissue culture dishes and selected with 2 μg/mL puromycin for 4 days prior to drug treatment. After selection, 40 million cells (8 plates each containing 5 million cells) were plated for each biological replicate, and an additional 40 million cells per replicate were collected and frozen for subsequent genomic DNA (gDNA) extraction. A549 and NCI-H460 cells were then treated with 1 μM M3541 versus DMSO control, for 19 days. Cells were re-plated every 3–4 days and maintained in drug or DMSO-containing media, each time plating a minimum of 40 million cells per replicate. At the end of the screen, the cells were harvested and frozen for gDNA extraction.

#### Genomic DNA preparation, sequencing and identification of top hits

gDNA was isolated using QIAGEN QIAamp DNA blood midi and maxi kits, according to manufacturer’s protocol. PCR of gDNA was performed to attach sequencing adaptors and barcode samples for sgRNA sequencing, as previously described (Doench et al., 2016). Samples were sequenced on an Illumina HiSeq2000. Reads per million were log2-transformed by first adding one to all values, which was necessary to take the log of sgRNAs with zero reads. For analysis, these normalized data were used to determine the log2-fold change of each sgRNA for the drug treatment group relative to DMSO control group (Shalem et al., 2014). The STARS gene-ranking algorithm was used to determine the top hits (https://portals.broadinstitute.org/gpp/public/software/stars); at least two sgRNAs targeting a gene had to rank within the top 10% of sgRNAs by log2-fold change in one direction or another (Doench et al., 2016). The hit genes were scored using the STARS score and the false discovery rate. Additionally, the normalized data were also analyzed with the hypergeometric distribution method (https://github.com/mhegde/volcano_plots). The volcano plots of these results were created using R (https://www.r-project.org).

#### Western blotting

Cells were lysed with lysis buffer [300 mM NaCl, 50 mM Tris-Cl (pH 7.4), 1 mM EDTA, 0.5% NP-40], lysates were resolved on denaturing Nu-page (Invitrogen) polyacrylamide gels and transferred onto nitrocellulose membranes. Membranes were blocked with 5% milk in TBST, and probed with primary and secondary antibodies respectively, then detected with chemiluminescence (Western Lightning, Perkin Elmer).

#### CRISPR cas9 Knockout

To generate A549, NCI-H460, HeLa and U2OS cells expressing the indicated sgRNAs, the oligonucleotides described in Table S1 were cloned into the pLentiCRISPR V2 viral vector.

Oligonucleotides used for sgRNA cloning are shown in the supplementary table (Table S3).

#### siRNA transfection

For siRNA transfection, cells were seeded at about 30% confluence into 6-well plates and transfected with a specific siRNA duplex using Lipofectamine RNAiMAX Reagent Agent (Life Technologies, #13778150) according to the manufacturer’s instructions for 48 hr. The sequences of the siRNAs used in this study are shown in the supplementary table (Key Resources Table and Table S3). SiRNA resistant CtIP plasmids are described previously (Chanut et al., 2016).

#### Clonogenic assay

Cells were seeded at a concentration of 1000–2500 cells per well into 6-well plates. After 24 hr, cells were continuously treated with indicated compounds for about 2 weeks. Colonies were fixed with fixation solution (5 parts methanol + 1 part acetic acid) at room temperature for 20 min and then stained with a solution of 0.5% crystal violet in methanol for 1 hour.

#### CellTiter-Glo assay

Cells were seeded into 96-well plates at a cell density of 3,000 cells per well, incubated overnight and treated with indicated compounds. The ATP-based, cell viability assay was carried out after incubation for 4 days (CellTiter-Glo, Promega). Survival curves were calculated by best-fit analysis of the log of the drug concentration to fold change of treated cells over vehicle-treated cells. All survival assays included technical triplicates.

#### Subcellular Fractionation

Subcellular fractions were isolated using a subcellular protein fractionation kit (Thermo Fisher Scientific) according to the manufacturer’s instructions, and the resultant fractions were analyzed with western blotting. Antibodies used in this study are listed in the Key Resources Table.

#### Comet assays

Alkaline comet assays were performed with manufacturer’s instruction (Trevigen). Cells were trypsinized and suspended in cold PBS at a concentration of 2.0 × 105 cells/ml. The cells were then mixed with low melting agarose (Trevigen) at a ratio of 1:10 (v/v) and immediately plated onto Cometslide (Trevigen). Alkaline electrophoresis was run at 25 V for 30 minutes in the electrophoresis system. Data were analyzed with a fluorescence microscope (Zeiss).

#### Reporter assays

NHEJ and HR efficiencies were measured using the EJ5-GFP and DR-GFP reporter assay, respectively (Ceccaldi et al., 2015). Briefly, 24 h before infection with I-Sce-I adenovirus, U2OS cells with either GFP expression cassette were transfected with the indicated siRNA and/or treated with ATMi (1 μM). The HR and NHEJ activity was determined by flow cytometric quantification of viable GFP-positive cells 72 h after I-Sce-I adenovirus infection.

#### Immunofluorescence

Cells plated on coverslips were washed once with PBS and fixed with 4% paraformaldehyde for 10 minutes on ice. 0.5% Triton X-100 was added to cells for 30 min for extraction. Coverslips were then blocked with 3% BSA for 30 min and incubated with primary antibody (diluted in 3% BSA) overnight. Following overnight incubation, coverslips were washed three times with PBST, then incubated with anti-rabbit secondary antibody (Alexa Fluor, Life Technologies) for 1 hour. Coverslips were then mounted with DAPI medium and visualized under the fluorescence microscope.

#### Cytogenetics

Cells were transfected with siRNAs twice for 48 h and incubated for 48 h in the presence or absence of 20 ng/ml MMC. Cells were exposed for 2 hours to colcemid (0.1μg/ml) and harvested using a 0.075M KCl hypotonic solution and fixed with 3:1 methanol: acetic acid. Slides were stained with Wright’s stain and when possible, 50 metaphase spreads were scored for aberrations. Metaphase spreads were observed using a Zeiss Axio Imager microscope and captured using CytoVision software from Applied Imaging.

#### SMART assay

Fiber comb assay was performed using the FiberComb machine (Genomic Vision). In brief, cells were treated with bromodeoxyuridine (BrdU, Sigma) for 24 hours. After 24-hour treatment with 1 μM ATMi, cells were then trypsinized, counted and embedded in low melting point agarose plugs, then treated with proteinase K overnight. Agarose plugs were then washed and digested with agarase. Agarase-treated samples were then poured into FiberComb wells and combed onto silanized coverslips. Coverslips were probed with rat anti-BrdU antibody (Abcam) and visualized by fluorescence microscopy. Pictures were taken of at least 100 fibers per condition. DNA fibers were measured with ImageJ and graphed. Each experiment was repeated at least three times unless otherwise stated.

#### In vitro DNA end resection

U2OS cells stably expressing HA-ER-AsiSI were created as described previously (Zhou et al., 2014). ssDNAs were quantitated by the HA-ER-AsiSI system in which AsiSI enzyme is fused to the estrogen receptor. The cells were treated with or without 300 nM 4-OHT for four hours to induce DSBs at specific AsiSI sites. Subsequently, genomic DNA was extracted with the QIAGEN DNeasy Blood & Tissue Kit and ssDNA at the specific AsiSI site in chromosome 1 was measured by qPCR with the primers as describing in Table S3.

#### Computational Analysis

Data from the Broad Institute Cancer Dependency Map Achilles CRISPR Avana 17Q2 dataset (Meyers et al., 2017), the Cancer Cell Line Encyclopedia (Cancer Cell Line Encyclopedia and Genomics of Drug Sensitivity in Cancer, 2015), the Genomics of Drug Sensitivity in Cancer (GDSC) (https://www.cancerrxgene.org/) (Yang et al., 2013), and the PanCancer MSK-IMPACT Clinical Sequencing Cohort (Zehir et al., 2017) were extracted for analysis. The MSK-IMPACT Clinical Sequencing Cohort and Cancer Cell Line Encyclopedia datasets were accessed through the public portal (http://www.cbioportal.org). For dependency analysis, copy number loss of genes was indicated by a copy number variation of −2 or −1 relative to diploid. Normal copy number was indicated by 0 variation relative to diploid. Copy number was chosen as a proxy for gene depletion because RAD18, FAAP24, and FAAP100 mutations are not screened for in cell lines. Cell lines that were in the first quartile of IC50 to a drug were categorized as sensitive and cell lines that were in the fourth quartile of IC50 were categorized as resistant. The cell lines ± one quartile from the median were not used in our analysis. For analysis of correlation between patient survival and mutations in ATM or FA genes, patient survival data was matched with FANCA, FANCC, and ATM mutation status using the PanCancer MSK-IMPACT Clinical Sequencing Cohort. The study only screened FANCA and FANCC mutations, commonly mutated FA genes. Due to the significant difference in timeline between groups for survival data, all data before 27.25 months (the last patient in the FA and ATM mutated group), was utilized and analyzed.

### QUANTITATION AND STATISTICAL ANALYSIS

All quantitative data were analyzed and graphed using Prism 7 GraphPad software. All data are represented as mean ± SEM calculated using the Prism software, unless indicated otherwise. Significance was tested using the non-parametric Mann-Whitney U Test unless indicated otherwise. Clinical data were analyzed using the Kaplan-Meier method and the log-rank (Mantel-Cox) regression test for significance.
